### Setup: Connecting the integral to the Laurent series of $e^{1/z}$

The Laurent series of $e^{1/z}$ on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ is

$$e^{1/z} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k!}\,z^{-k}, \qquad |z|>0.$$

The coefficient of $z^{-n}$ is $a_{-n} = \tfrac{1}{n!}$, extracted by the standard contour-integral formula

$$a_{-n} = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|z|=1} e^{1/z}\,z^{\,n-1}\,dz. \tag{1}$$

### Parametrizing the contour integral

Set $z = e^{i\theta}$, $\theta\in[0,2\pi]$, so $dz = ie^{i\theta}\,d\theta$ and $1/z = e^{-i\theta} = \cos\theta - i\sin\theta$. Then

$$e^{1/z}\,z^{n-1}\,dz = e^{e^{-i\theta}}\,e^{i(n-1)\theta}\cdot ie^{i\theta}\,d\theta = i\,e^{e^{-i\theta}}\,e^{in\theta}\,d\theta.$$

Substituting into (1):

$$\frac{1}{n!} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} e^{e^{-i\theta}}\,e^{in\theta}\,d\theta. \tag{2}$$

### Taking the real part

Since $e^{-i\theta} = \cos\theta - i\sin\theta$,

$$e^{e^{-i\theta}}\,e^{in\theta} = e^{\cos\theta}\,e^{-i\sin\theta}\,e^{in\theta} = e^{\cos\theta}\,e^{i(n\theta - \sin\theta)}.$$

Its real part is

$$\operatorname{Re}\!\bigl(e^{e^{-i\theta}}\,e^{in\theta}\bigr) = e^{\cos\theta}\cos(n\theta - \sin\theta) = e^{\cos\theta}\cos(\sin\theta - n\theta),$$

using the evenness of cosine. The imaginary part is $-e^{\cos\theta}\sin(\sin\theta-n\theta)$, which is an odd function about $\theta=\pi$ (one checks $h(2\pi-\theta)=-h(\theta)$), so its integral over $[0,2\pi]$ vanishes. Since $\tfrac{1}{n!}$ is real, (2) gives

$$\frac{1}{n!} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} e^{\cos\theta}\cos(\sin\theta - n\theta)\,d\theta. \tag{3}$$

### Reducing $[0,2\pi]$ to $[0,\pi]$

Let $g(\theta) = e^{\cos\theta}\cos(\sin\theta - n\theta)$. Using $\cos(2\pi-\theta)=\cos\theta$, $\sin(2\pi-\theta)=-\sin\theta$:

$$g(2\pi-\theta) = e^{\cos\theta}\cos(-\sin\theta - 2n\pi + n\theta) = e^{\cos\theta}\cos(n\theta-\sin\theta) = g(\theta).$$

So $g$ is symmetric about $\theta = \pi$, hence

$$\int_0^{2\pi} g(\theta)\,d\theta = 2\int_0^{\pi} g(\theta)\,d\theta.$$

Substituting into (3):

$$\frac{1}{n!} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot 2\int_0^{\pi} e^{\cos\theta}\cos(\sin\theta - n\theta)\,d\theta = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} e^{\cos\theta}\cos(\sin\theta - n\theta)\,d\theta = I_n.$$

### Result

$$\boxed{I_n = \frac{1}{n!}}, \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$$

The mechanism: the substitution $z = e^{i\theta}$ turns the Laurent coefficient $a_{-n}=\tfrac{1}{n!}$ of $e^{1/z}$ into the Fourier coefficient of $e^{e^{-i\theta}}$, and orthogonality (equivalently, the contour-integral extraction formula) isolates exactly the $\tfrac{1}{n!}$ term.
